texts.title: Why is the night sky dark?

paragraphs.text: It seems obvious why the sky is dark at night: the sun has set. Yet for several centuries this simple fact posed a genuine puzzle for astronomers, and its resolution turned out to reveal something profound about the universe. If the universe were infinite, unchanging and filled evenly with stars, every line of sight from the Earth would eventually end on the surface of a star, and the whole night sky should blaze as brightly as the surface of the sun. The fact that it does not became known as the Olbers paradox, after a German astronomer who described it in the 1820s, although others had noticed the problem earlier. The question was discussed by several astronomers before him, including one in the sixteenth century.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The argument is simpler than it first appears. Distant stars appear fainter than nearby ones, since their light spreads out over a larger area as it travels. But if stars are scattered evenly through space, the number of stars at any given distance increases in exactly the same proportion as the brightness of each one decreases. Each shell of space around the Earth, however far away, should therefore contribute the same amount of light, and an infinite number of such shells would produce an extremely bright sky, as bright as the surface of a star once nearer stars block those behind them. The same reasoning applies to a forest: stand in a large enough wood and every line of sight ends on a tree trunk.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Several early explanations proved inadequate. One suggested that clouds of dust between the stars absorb the light of distant ones. But dust that absorbed so much light would itself be heated until it glowed as brightly as the stars, so absorption cannot solve the problem. Another suggestion was that the stars are not spread evenly but arranged in a hierarchy of clusters within clusters, leaving large empty regions. This idea could in principle reduce the brightness of the sky, but observations did not support the particular arrangement it required. Some astronomers also argued that the universe contained only a limited number of stars, but this conflicted with the widespread belief in an infinite and eternal cosmos.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The real explanation depends on two facts established in the twentieth century. The first is that the universe has a finite age, estimated at around 13.8 billion years. Light travels at a finite speed, so we can see only the light that has had time to reach us since the universe began, which comes from a limited region of space. However large the universe may be beyond that region, its light has not yet arrived. The stars we can see are therefore not infinite in number, and their combined light is far too small to fill the sky. This limit is sometimes called the observable universe; even if the universe is infinite in size, the light from its most distant parts is still on its way.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The second fact is that the universe is expanding. As light travels across expanding space, its wavelength is stretched, shifting it towards the red end of the spectrum and reducing its energy. Light from very distant sources arrives much weaker than it would in a static universe, and some of it has been stretched so far that it is no longer visible at all. Both effects work in the same direction, and together they explain why darkness prevails between the stars. The stretching of light is measured by astronomers as a redshift.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Remarkably, a solution along these lines was suggested in the nineteenth century by an unexpected figure. The American writer Edgar Allan Poe proposed, in a long prose poem published in 1848, that the gaps between stars appear dark because light from the most distant regions has not yet had time to reach us. Poe had no scientific evidence for his claim, and it attracted little attention from astronomers of the time, but historians of science regard it as a striking anticipation of the modern answer. The poem also contained many ideas that later proved wrong.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The night sky is not, in fact, completely dark. In every direction there is a faint glow of microwave radiation left over from the early universe, when all of space was hot and bright. Had we eyes sensitive to microwaves, the sky would appear evenly lit. This radiation, discovered by accident in the 1960s by two engineers who were trying to eliminate an unexplained source of noise in a radio antenna, is itself the stretched light of a time when the whole universe glowed, and it provides some of the strongest evidence for the modern account of cosmic history. The two engineers at first suspected that birds nesting in the antenna were responsible for the noise.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The Olbers paradox is sometimes presented as a curiosity, but its lesson is significant. A question that anyone can ask by looking up at night leads directly to the conclusion that the universe had a beginning and is changing over time. The darkness between the stars, in other words, is not merely the absence of light; it is evidence about the history of everything. Few everyday observations carry so much meaning.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Plastic is one of the most useful materials ever invented and one of the most difficult to dispose of. It is light, strong, cheap and can be shaped into almost anything, and global production has grown from a few million tonnes in the 1950s to several hundred million tonnes a year today. Yet only a small fraction of the plastic ever made has been recycled. Most has been burned, buried in landfill or has escaped into the environment, where it can persist for centuries, breaking into ever smaller fragments without truly disappearing. Some of it ends up in the oceans, where fragments have been found in animals from plankton to whales, and production is expected to continue growing for decades.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The main reason recycling rates are low is that plastics are not one material but many. Bottles, food trays, carrier bags and car parts are made from different polymers, long chains of molecules with different properties, and they cannot usually be recycled together. Many products combine several plastics, or plastic with paper, metal or other materials, making separation difficult or impossible. Colours, labels, food residues and additives further reduce the value of what is collected. Even the same type of plastic may contain different additives that make recycling more difficult, and some plastics, such as those used in electrical fittings, cannot be melted and reshaped at all.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Most recycling today is mechanical. Collected plastic is sorted, washed, shredded and melted, and the molten material is formed into pellets that can be used to make new products. Modern sorting facilities use infrared light to identify different polymers on fast-moving conveyor belts and jets of air to separate them. Mechanical recycling works well for some materials, particularly the clear plastic used for drinks bottles, but each cycle of melting shortens the polymer chains and reduces quality, so that recycled plastic is often turned into lower-grade products, such as fibres for clothing or garden furniture, rather than back into bottles. Clear bottles are the most valuable material, while coloured and black plastics are often harder to sort, and the purity of the collected material largely determines its price.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Chemical recycling aims to overcome these limits by breaking plastics down into their chemical building blocks or into oils that can be used to make new plastic of the same quality as the original. Several methods exist, from heating plastic without oxygen to using solvents or enzymes that dissolve particular polymers. In principle, chemical recycling could handle mixed and contaminated plastics that mechanical methods cannot. In practice, most plants operating so far are small, use a lot of energy, and turn much of their input into fuel rather than new plastic, which critics argue should not count as recycling at all. Supporters argue that chemical recycling could complement mechanical methods rather than compete with them.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Enzymes have attracted particular attention. In 2016, researchers in Japan identified a bacterium, found near a bottle recycling site, that had evolved the ability to digest the plastic used in drinks bottles. Scientists have since engineered improved versions of its enzymes that work far faster, and one company has built a demonstration plant that breaks down bottles and textiles into their original components. Enzymes work only on certain types of plastic, however, and scaling up the process remains expensive. The bacterium was discovered during a search for organisms living on plastic waste, and other researchers are looking for enzymes that can break down different plastics.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Design is increasingly seen as just as important as recycling technology. Products made from a single type of plastic, without unnecessary colours or labels, are much easier to recycle, and some manufacturers have simplified their packaging accordingly. Deposit schemes, in which customers pay a small sum when buying a drink and receive it back when they return the empty container, have achieved return rates above ninety per cent in some countries, producing clean, well-sorted material that is valuable to recyclers. Some countries also tax plastic packaging that contains little recycled material, and refill systems, in which containers are returned and reused rather than recycled, are also being tested.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Trade has complicated the picture. For many years, wealthy countries exported much of their collected plastic to countries in Asia, where it was often processed in poor conditions or dumped. When the largest importer banned most such imports in 2018, recycling systems elsewhere were thrown into crisis, and some collected plastic was burned or sent to landfill instead. The episode revealed that some reported recycling rates had measured what was collected rather than what was actually turned into new products. Several other countries later introduced similar restrictions.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Most experts agree that recycling alone cannot solve the problem of plastic waste. Reducing unnecessary use, designing products for reuse and making manufacturers responsible for what happens to their packaging are all needed as well. Recycling nonetheless remains an essential part of the answer, and improvements in sorting, chemistry and design may yet allow a much larger share of plastic to be kept in use rather than thrown away. Consumers, too, have a part to play, although individual choices alone cannot solve a problem created by entire industries.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Do we still need animals in medical research?

paragraphs.text: For more than a century, most new medicines have been tested on animals before being given to people. Mice, rats and, less often, dogs and monkeys are used to study how diseases develop, to check whether new drugs are safe and to estimate what doses might be appropriate. Millions of animals are used in research each year worldwide. The practice has always been controversial, and in recent years scientific developments and changes in law have raised the question of whether it is still necessary, or whether alternatives are now good enough to replace it. Mice account for the great majority of animals used, and few questions in science provoke such strong feelings on both sides.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Defenders of animal research point to its contribution to medicine. Vaccines, antibiotics, transplant surgery, insulin treatment and many cancer drugs were developed with the help of experiments on animals, which allow researchers to study the effects of a treatment on a whole living body, with all its interacting organs, in a way that cells in a dish cannot. Elena Vasquez, a pharmacologist, argues that some questions, such as how a drug is absorbed, distributed and broken down in the body, can at present be answered reliably only in living organisms. Most of the drugs in use today were tested on animals at some stage, and some researchers add that animal studies have also been essential in veterinary medicine, benefiting animals themselves.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Critics question how well animal results predict human responses. A large proportion of drugs that appear safe and effective in animals fail when tested in people, either because they do not work or because they cause harmful effects that did not appear in the animal studies. Martin Okonkwo, who studies animal welfare, argues that differences between species mean that animal tests can be misleading in both directions: some useful drugs may have been abandoned because they harmed animals, while some harmful ones passed animal tests. He also notes that laboratory animals live in conditions very different from those of human patients, which may affect results. Some diseases that affect humans do not occur naturally in other species at all, so they must be imitated artificially.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Alternatives have advanced rapidly. Researchers can now grow miniature, simplified versions of human organs, known as organoids, from stem cells, and build organ-on-a-chip devices in which human cells are arranged in tiny channels that imitate blood flow and the connections between organs. Computer models can predict some toxic effects from the chemical structure of a substance. Julia Stein, a toxicologist, says that for certain tests, such as whether a chemical irritates the skin or eyes, these methods have already replaced animal tests in many countries and in some cases perform better. Such devices can also be built from the cells of individual patients, raising the prospect of testing drugs on the tissue of a particular person before treatment.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Stein cautions, however, that no current alternative can reproduce the full complexity of a living body, including the immune system, hormones and the interactions between many organs over time. For long-term effects, effects on pregnancy and development, and complex diseases, she believes animal studies will remain necessary for some years. She argues that alternatives are best seen as a way of reducing and refining animal use rather than, for now, eliminating it. She adds that combining several different methods may eventually provide the same information as an animal study, although developing and validating each new method can take many years.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Law and regulation are changing. For decades, regulators in many countries required animal testing before a new drug could be tried in humans. Some have recently removed this requirement, allowing companies to submit evidence from non-animal methods instead where it is considered adequate, and several have announced plans to reduce animal testing substantially over the coming decades. Cosmetics testing on animals has been banned in a number of regions. Some regulators are also funding research to validate new methods, and some companies now use non-animal methods for most of their safety testing.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The ethical debate is not only about effectiveness. Rahul Menon, a bioethicist, points out that even if animal research were perfectly predictive, it would still raise the question of whether it is right to cause suffering to animals for human benefit. He supports the widely used principles known as the three Rs: replacing animals where possible, reducing the numbers used and refining procedures to minimise suffering. But he argues that these principles have too often been applied as a matter of form rather than substance, and that funding for alternatives remains small compared with the sums spent on research using animals. Public attitudes vary widely between countries and have shifted over time.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The most likely future is gradual change rather than sudden abolition. Animal research is likely to decline as alternatives improve and regulators accept them, first for simpler tests and later, perhaps, for more complex ones. Whether it disappears entirely will depend on scientific progress that cannot yet be predicted, and on how societies weigh the interests of animals against the benefits to human health. Scientists on both sides of the debate agree that better methods would be welcome.
paragraphs.label: H
